messages.author: d5ae607f2255e054
messages.subject: Standardizing observation covariates
parts:
Hello all,

 

I'm sorry if this question has been answered, but I can't seem to find an explanation. I am building a n-mixture removal model with both site and observation covariates. We are interested in incorporating day of year (doy) into the detection model as a proxy to leafout conditions as the surveys took place from spring to early summer. We expect to see a decrease in detection as doy increases. I understand the importance of standardizing continuous variables, but I am unsure how to approach it with observation covariates specifically. For my example, I'll include a portion of the first line of data, but there are 57 sites and up to 8 survey events.

 

Shown below is an example of doy values for one site

              1          2        3          4         5         6

1         122     124     131     133     137      ...

2          ...

 

I have seen 2 different methods used in various tutorials and examples. 

 

scale(data[,c(1:6)]) which standardizes by survey event (each column).

            1                    2                      3                      4                     5

-0.71665004 -1.77807859 -1.25370502 -1.351981676 -1.25656001

 

And the standardize function from wiqid package.

 

standardize(as.matrix(data[,c(1:6)]))

 

This calculates a single mean and standard deviation for all the survey events and applies it to each column. Which gives results like this 

           1                   2                   3                      4                 5

-1.6601355 -1.4703218 -0.80597377 -0.61616004 -0.2365326

 

The method I use definitely changes my results, so I want to make sure I'm using the correct one. The first method seems to fit the data better, but the second makes more sense to me. I was hoping for an explanation on why one would use one method over the other method. Is one more correct than the other?

 

Sincerely,

 Jena

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing observation covariates
parts:
Dear Jena,

I think you need to standardize the full matrix with a single value for mean and sd. Standardizing by occasion/survey events would not make much sense in my opinion in your case.

In general I would always standardize with a single pair of mean and sd for a covariate. Exception might be something like day of year when modeling data from multiple years. If whatever affects detection, and which is correlated with date, varies quite a bit from year to year, then it might make sense to center date for each year on a separate value. Let's say you count some white species in some place where there is a snowcover in the winter. In that situation, you might center date in each year separately, by subtracting the average date of snowmelt from each date. A negative value of date then corresponds to a date when the landscape is still white, while a positive value means the white animals should be pretty visible in a brown or green landscape.

That is, by centering on snowmelt, you make date a much better proxy for what really matters for detection. (On the other hand, one could then also add a binary variable "pre- vs. post-snowmelt" into detection...).

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.author: 97512b0c9bacfbef
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing observation covariates
parts:
Jena, good question, and Marc, thanks for your reply.  

I have a similar situation - multiple surveys per year over multiple years, with day-of-year (DOY) included as an observation covariate.  I also included cumulative degree days as an observation covariate, as a continuous variable to measure the progress of spring.  However, our study subjects are amphibian egg masses laid in vernal pools, and the timing of egg-laying is likely a complex phenomenon, likely in some way related to degree days (soil, water, and air temps).  I've been including DOY to account for effects of spring's progress beyond thermal conditions which are captured in cumulative degree days.

Jena, if you know leaf-out correlates to cumulative degree days, this might perhaps be a better proxy and could be scaled across all years if I understand Marc correctly.

-Alex

parts:
Marc and Alex,

Thank you both for the fast responses! 

Marc, your explanation was very helpful. My data is in fact spread across multiple years and each of those years the surveys took place in a different watershed. I know one year was very wet and another was very dry, so I can easily see this affecting leafout. Some of these watersheds are at higher lattitude than the others as well, so I do think it would vary based on both year and location. 

Alex, thanks for the suggestion! Cumulative degree days could potentially account for the seasonal differences in location. My study species is a turtle, so we're also very interested in thermal conditions. 

I will have to try both suggestions.

Thank you,
Jena
